lessons.title: The Invisible Killer in the Rock: Nuclear Structure, Isotopes & Launching the Phenomenon

quiz.prompt: A photographic film was sealed in a lightproof box next to a piece of pitchblende (uranium ore) in a dark room. When the film was developed, it showed a clear image. No light, heat or sound was involved. Which statement is supported by this observation alone?
choices: The film was exposed by sound made by the rock.
A hidden lamp inside the box lit up the film.
Something from the rock reached the film even though no light could enter the box.
Heat from the rock burned the film.
quiz.rationale: The observation only shows that something invisible passed from the rock to the film. The cause is not yet explained, and light, heat and sound were ruled out.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share on the pitchblende film photograph ('found in a geology lab in Nairobi')

quiz.prompt: During the prediction activity, learners' ideas about what came out of the rock are written word-for-word in the 'Before' column of the class anchor chart. What happens to these predictions?
choices: They are kept without correction and revisited in later lessons as new evidence is gathered.
Only the predictions that turn out to be correct are kept.
They are marked right or wrong straight away by the teacher.
They are erased once the teacher gives the correct answer.
quiz.rationale: The predictions are a record of the class's starting ideas. They are not corrected on the day and are revisited every lesson, as the teacher says.
quiz.placement: Predict: cold-call predictions scribed on the 'Before' column of the class anchor chart

quiz.prompt: Uranium-238 has atomic number Z = 92 and mass number A = 238. How many neutrons (N) are in one nucleus of uranium-238?
quiz.rationale: Neutron number N = A − Z = 238 − 92 = 146.
quiz.placement: Observe: completing the N column of the 10-nuclide data table ('Show me how you calculated N for Uranium-238')

quiz.prompt: Carbon-12 (mass number 12) and carbon-14 (mass number 14) both have atomic number Z = 6. Which statement correctly compares them?
choices: They have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons.
They have the same number of protons (6) but different numbers of neutrons (6 and 8).
Carbon-14 has 14 protons and carbon-12 has 12 protons.
They are different elements because their mass numbers are different.
quiz.rationale: Z = 6 means 6 protons in both. N = A − Z gives 6 neutrons in carbon-12 and 8 neutrons in carbon-14, so they are isotopes of the same element.
quiz.placement: Observe: reading 'Inside the Rock' and plotting Carbon-12 (Z = 6, N = 6) and Carbon-14 (Z = 6, N = 8) on the N vs Z graph

quiz.prompt: Learners plotted many nuclides on a graph with neutron number N on the y-axis and proton number Z on the x-axis, with the line N = Z drawn. Which description best matches where the stable nuclides cluster?
choices: In a band that curves above the N = Z line for heavier elements.
In a band that curves below the N = Z line for heavier elements.
Spread evenly all over the graph with no pattern.
Exactly on the N = Z line for every element.
quiz.rationale: The stable nuclides form a band called the belt of stability. For heavier elements the band moves above the N = Z line because stable heavy nuclei have more neutrons than protons.
quiz.placement: Observe: groups shade the belt of stability on the pre-printed N vs Z graph and circle the outsiders

quiz.prompt: The Kericho runners analogy says isotopes are like two runners where one carries an extra weight. Carbon-13 has 6 protons and 7 neutrons, and it is a stable isotope of carbon. What does this show about the analogy?
choices: Neutrons only make a nucleus lighter, never heavier.
Extra neutrons do not automatically make a nucleus unstable, so the 'extra weight' idea has limits.
Carbon-13 must really be radioactive, because it has extra neutrons.
Any isotope with more neutrons than carbon-12 is unstable.
quiz.rationale: Carbon-13 has more neutrons than carbon-12 but is stable. Stability depends on the balance of forces in the nucleus, not just on carrying extra neutrons.
quiz.placement: Observe: Kericho runners isotope analogy and the teacher's 'limit of the analogy' statement

quiz.prompt: In the Driving Question Board activity, learners write questions about pitchblende and radioactivity that they cannot yet answer. Which question is the most investigable?
choices: Do you think the pitchblende rock is beautiful?
Why do scientists like rocks?
Is radioactivity scary?
How does the darkening of a film change when the same ore is placed closer to or further from it?
quiz.rationale: This question can be tested by changing one variable (distance) and observing the film. The other questions are matters of opinion or are too vague to investigate.
quiz.placement: DQB: writing three sticky-note questions and posting them in the columns of the Driving Question Board

lessons.title: Types of Radiation: Alpha, Beta, and Gamma — Penetrating Power and Nuclear Identity

quiz.prompt: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation are each directed at sheets of paper, aluminium foil and lead. Which list shows the radiations from LEAST penetrating to MOST penetrating?
choices: Alpha, gamma, beta
Alpha, beta, gamma
Gamma, beta, alpha
Beta, alpha, gamma
quiz.rationale: Alpha is stopped by paper, beta needs aluminium foil, and gamma is only reduced by thick lead. So penetrating power increases from alpha to beta to gamma.
quiz.placement: Radiation Penetration Diagram Set and Evidence Table (Stopped By column)

quiz.prompt: Alpha particles are the MOST strongly ionising radiation, yet a sheet of paper stops them. What is the best explanation?
choices: They lose their energy quickly because they ionise very many atoms along a short path
Alpha particles are much lighter than beta particles, so they are easily stopped
Strong ionisation means an alpha particle has extra energy left over to keep travelling through matter
Alpha particles have no charge, so they are easily blocked by solid materials
quiz.rationale: Each ionisation uses up some of the particle's energy. An alpha particle ionises so many atoms that it runs out of energy within a very short distance. Ionising ability and penetrating power are therefore opposite.
quiz.placement: Evidence Table check: ionising ability versus penetrating power (misconception pause)

quiz.prompt: Radium-226 (atomic number 86 + 2 = 88, mass number 226) undergoes alpha decay. Which daughter nucleus is formed?
choices: Radon-222 (atomic number 86)
Francium-226 (atomic number 87)
Thorium-230 (atomic number 90)
Radon-226 (atomic number 86)
quiz.rationale: An alpha particle removes 4 from the mass number and 2 from the atomic number. This gives mass number 226 - 4 = 222 and atomic number 88 - 2 = 86, which is radon-222.
quiz.placement: Part A: Nuclear Decay Equations, unguided equation (1) Radium-226

quiz.prompt: Carbon-14 (atomic number 6, mass number 14) undergoes beta-minus decay. Which daughter nucleus is formed?
choices: Boron-14 (atomic number 5)
Nitrogen-14 (atomic number 7)
Carbon-13 (atomic number 6)
Beryllium-10 (atomic number 4)
quiz.rationale: Beta-minus emission raises the atomic number by 1 and leaves the mass number unchanged. This gives atomic number 7 and mass number 14, which is nitrogen-14.
quiz.placement: Part A: Nuclear Decay Equations, unguided equation (2) Carbon-14

quiz.prompt: Uranium-238 (atomic number 92) emits an alpha particle and becomes thorium-234 (atomic number 90). How many neutrons does a thorium-234 nucleus have?
quiz.rationale: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 234 - 90 = 144. Uranium-238 had 146 neutrons, so it lost 2 neutrons and 2 protons in the alpha particle.
quiz.placement: Part B: Connecting Back to the Rock, comparing U-238 (146/92) with Th-234 (144/90)

quiz.prompt: On a graph of N (neutrons, vertical axis) against Z (protons, horizontal axis), a nucleus undergoes beta-minus decay. How does its position move?
choices: Up and to the left, because N increases by 1 and Z decreases by 1
It does not move, because the mass number stays the same
Down and to the right, because N decreases by 1 and Z increases by 1
Down and to the left, because N decreases by 2 and Z decreases by 2
quiz.rationale: In beta-minus decay a neutron changes into a proton. So N goes down by 1 and Z goes up by 1, which is a diagonal step down and to the right. The first option describes alpha decay.
quiz.placement: Part B: Connecting Back to the Rock, blue arrows for beta decay on the N vs Z plot

quiz.prompt: A piece of pitchblende is placed on photographic film inside a lightproof paper-and-card box. The film is exposed. Which explanation fits the evidence on penetrating power?
choices: Alpha particles from uranium-238 pass through the box and expose the film
Only gamma radiation exists in pitchblende, so no other radiation is emitted
Beta and gamma radiation from the unstable daughter nuclei pass through the box, while alpha is stopped by paper or card
The film is exposed by light that leaks into the box, not by radiation
quiz.rationale: Alpha particles are stopped by paper or card, so they cannot reach the film. Beta and gamma radiation, emitted by daughters such as thorium-234 and protactinium-234, are penetrating enough to get through and expose it.
quiz.placement: Part B: Connecting Back to the Rock, link back to the film in the lightproof box

quiz.prompt: Uranium-238 has N/Z = 146/92 ≈ 1.59. After one alpha decay it becomes thorium-234 with N/Z = 144/90 = 1.60. Which statement best fits this evidence about the uranium-238 decay chain?
choices: This first alpha step does not necessarily bring the nucleus closer to the belt, but the whole chain ends at stable lead-206
Every alpha emission moves a nucleus closer to the belt of stability, so the chain stops after one step
The chain never ends because beta emission always makes nuclei less stable
The chain ends at thorium-234 because gamma emission makes it stable
quiz.rationale: The N/Z ratio does not move closer to the belt after the first alpha step (1.59 to 1.60). Alpha emission mainly reduces the size of a heavy nucleus, and the full chain of alpha and beta decays finally reaches stable lead-206.
quiz.placement: Cumulative Nuclear Stability Model: decay arrows for U-238 → Th-234 → Pa-234 on the N vs Z poster

lessons.title: Detection of Radiation: Seeing the Invisible

quiz.prompt: In a Geiger-Müller (GM) counter simulation, there is no radioactive source anywhere near the tube, yet the counter still clicks about 20 times in 30 seconds. What is the best explanation?
choices: The clicks are caused by light entering the tube
The GM tube produces its own radiation when it is switched on
The counter is faulty and should be replaced
The tube detects background radiation from natural sources such as cosmic rays, rocks and soil
quiz.rationale: Radiation is always present at a low level from cosmic rays, radon, rocks, building materials and food, so a GM tube clicks even with no source present. This is called background radiation.
quiz.placement: Part A: Virtual GM Counter, (i) Background radiation count with no source

quiz.prompt: A GM counter gives a high count rate near a radioactive source. When a single sheet of paper is placed between the source and the tube, the count rate drops to the background level. Which type of radiation does the source emit?
choices: Beta particles only
Gamma rays only
Alpha particles
Gamma rays and beta particles
quiz.rationale: Alpha particles are heavy and strongly ionising, so they have a very short range and are stopped by paper. Beta particles need aluminium to be reduced, and gamma rays pass through paper.
quiz.placement: Part A: Virtual GM Counter, (iii) Shielding test with paper, aluminium and lead

quiz.prompt: Which sequence correctly explains how a GM tube produces a 'click' when radiation enters it?
choices: Radiation heats the argon gas, the gas expands, and the expansion is counted as a click
Radiation enters the mica window and ionises argon atoms, the freed electrons accelerate to the central electrode and cause an avalanche, and the resulting electrical pulse is counted
Radiation makes the argon gas glow, and a light sensor in the counter detects the glow
Radiation melts the mica window, which completes the circuit and gives a click
quiz.rationale: Ionising radiation frees electrons from argon atoms. The high voltage accelerates them towards the central electrode, producing an avalanche of electrons that gives one pulse, and the counter registers one click.
quiz.placement: Part A: GM Tube Working Principle (claim–evidence–reasoning discussion)

quiz.prompt: In a cloud chamber, an alpha particle leaves a thick, straight track. Which explanation fits best?
choices: Alpha particles are very light, so nothing bends their path
Alpha particles are heavy and cause a lot of ionisation along their path, so the track is thick and they are not easily deflected
Alpha particles are electrically neutral, so they leave a wide trail
Alpha particles are a type of light, so they travel in straight lines
quiz.rationale: Alpha particles are heavy and strongly ionising, so they leave a dense, thick trail of ionisation and travel in a fairly straight line. Light beta particles are deflected more easily and leave thinner, curved tracks.
quiz.placement: Part B: Cloud Chamber video, sketching alpha, beta and gamma tracks

quiz.prompt: A positively charged leaf electroscope has its leaf standing out. When a radioactive source is brought near the cap, the leaf slowly falls. Why?
choices: The radiation adds more charge of the same sign to the leaf
The radiation ionises the air, and the ions carry the charge away from the electroscope
The radiation pushes the leaf down with a force like wind
The radiation heats the metal leaf and makes it limp
quiz.rationale: Radiation ionises the air around the cap. The ions carry the charge away, so the electroscope discharges and the leaf falls. This is another effect of ionisation.
quiz.placement: Part B: Leaf electroscope demonstration and the detection summary table

quiz.prompt: A GM counter in a Nairobi classroom picks up some counts even with no source present. Which of these is a natural source of that background radiation?
choices: Sound waves from the street outside
The heat from learners' bodies
Cosmic rays from space and radon gas from the soil
Light from the classroom bulbs
quiz.rationale: Background radiation comes from cosmic rays, radon gas, radioactive isotopes in rocks such as granite and building materials, and trace isotopes such as potassium-40 in food. Light, sound and body heat are not ionising radiation from unstable nuclei.
quiz.placement: Part B: Background Radiation Explanation, 'Where is the radiation coming from if there is no source?'

quiz.prompt: A pitchblende rock emits alpha, beta and gamma radiation. A GM tube is placed a few centimetres away in air. Which statement correctly describes what is detected?
choices: Gamma rays are stopped by the air gap, while alpha rays pass through easily
Alpha passes through the rock and air most easily, so it is detected most
Gamma rays pass through most barriers and are detected, while alpha is stopped by the rock itself and the air gap
All three types reach the tube equally, because the tube has a window
quiz.rationale: Gamma rays are the most penetrating, beta is partly absorbed, and alpha is stopped by the rock and a few centimetres of air. Reversing alpha and gamma penetration is a common misconception.
quiz.placement: Detection Layer added to the cumulative nuclear model (GM tube with dotted penetration arrows)

lessons.title: Half-Life and Decay Curves: How Long Before the Rock Goes Quiet?

quiz.prompt: In the dice simulation, 100 dice are rolled and every die showing 6 is removed. In Round 1, 17 dice are removed. In Round 3, only 12 are removed. Why does the number removed fall from round to round?
choices: The dice slowly become less likely to land on 6 as they are rolled more times
The probability of a 6 drops by a fixed amount each round
The dice that are left have used up some of their chance of decaying
Fewer dice are left to roll, and each remaining die still has the same 1-in-6 chance of being removed
quiz.rationale: The chance for each die stays 1 in 6, but there are fewer dice to roll, so fewer 6s appear. In the same way, fewer nuclei decay per unit time as the sample shrinks, even though each nucleus has a constant chance of decaying.
quiz.placement: Observe: dice simulation, pause at round 3 ('Does the number removed each round stay the same or change?')

quiz.prompt: A radioactive sample has 80 undecayed nuclei at time 0. A decay curve for it shows 40 nuclei left at 6 days and 20 nuclei left at 12 days. What is the half-life of the sample?
choices: 6 days
3 days
12 days
40 days
quiz.rationale: Half-life is the time for the number of undecayed nuclei to fall to half. The number falls from 80 to 40 in 6 days, so the half-life is 6 days. It halves again from 40 to 20 in the next 6 days.
quiz.placement: Observe: plotting the decay curve and reading off the half-life (dashed line at 50 dice remaining)

quiz.prompt: One group starts the dice simulation with 100 dice. Another group starts with 200 dice. Each die still has a 1-in-6 chance of being removed on every roll. Compared with the group with 100 dice, what will the group with 200 dice find for its half-life in rolls?
choices: About the same number of rolls, because half-life does not depend on the starting number
Exactly the same number of dice removed in every round
About twice as long, because there are twice as many dice to remove
About half as long, because more dice means more 6s per roll
quiz.rationale: Half-life depends only on the chance of decay for each nucleus (or die), not on the size of the sample. Both groups should find about 3.8 rolls, even though the 200-dice group removes more dice per round.
quiz.placement: Observe: formative question 'If you started with 200 dice, would your half-life change?'

quiz.prompt: Different groups did the same dice simulation and got slightly different decay curves, but all of them found a half-life of about 3 to 5 rolls. What does this tell us about radioactive decay?
choices: Decay is not random, because every group got the same curve
Decay of a single nucleus cannot be predicted, but the behaviour of a large number of nuclei follows a predictable pattern
Each nucleus chooses when to decay, so every sample behaves differently
The results are only reliable if the dice are rolled in the same order
quiz.rationale: Decay is random and spontaneous for each nucleus, so individual results scatter between groups. A large number of nuclei shows a consistent statistical pattern, which is why half-life is a reliable value.
quiz.placement: Observe: comparing curves and half-life values across groups ('What does the scatter tell us about individual nuclei?')

quiz.prompt: Archaeologists at Lukenya Hill in Machakos County find a charcoal fragment. It contains only one-eighth of the Carbon-14 activity of a living tree. The half-life of Carbon-14 is 5730 years. About how old is the charcoal?
choices: 11 460 years
716 years
17 190 years
45 840 years
quiz.rationale: One-eighth = (1/2)^3, so n = 3 half-lives have passed. Age = 3 x 5730 = 17 190 years.
quiz.placement: Explain: Problem 1 (Carbon dating at Lukenya Hill)

quiz.prompt: A patient at Kenyatta National Hospital is given Iodine-131, which has a half-life of 8 days. The dose starts with 8000 undecayed nuclei (simplified unit). How many undecayed nuclei remain after 32 days?
quiz.rationale: n = 32 / 8 = 4 half-lives. N = 8000 x (1/2)^4 = 8000 / 16 = 500. Dividing 8000 by 4 (giving 2000) is the common error of dividing by n instead of halving n times.
quiz.placement: Explain: Problem 2 (Iodine-131 at KNH)

quiz.prompt: Uranium-238 in the pitchblende rock has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years. Which statement best explains why the rock still gives off radiation today?
choices: Uranium-238 nuclei decay very slowly, so an enormous number of undecayed nuclei are still left to decay
The rock will stop emitting radiation very soon, because a half-life only lasts a short time
Uranium-238 never decays, so the rock can never run out of radiation
The rock keeps making new uranium-238 atoms to replace those that decay
quiz.rationale: A very long half-life means a very low decay rate for the whole sample. Even after billions of years, about half of the original nuclei are still undecayed, so the rock stays radioactive on a human timescale. The uranium does decay; it is not permanent.
quiz.placement: Explain: journal paragraph connecting half-life to the pitchblende rock ('Uranium-238 has a half-life of approximately 4.5 billion years, which means...')

quiz.prompt: A group sketches a decay curve of the number of undecayed nuclei (vertical axis) against time (horizontal axis) for a radioactive sample. Which description of the curve is correct?
choices: A horizontal line, because the number of nuclei stays the same
A curve that falls steeply at first and then flattens out, halving in each equal half-life interval
A curve that rises steadily as the nuclei decay
A straight line sloping down to zero at a steady rate
quiz.rationale: The number of nuclei halves in each half-life. The fall is therefore large at the start and gets smaller as fewer nuclei are left, giving an exponential decrease rather than a straight line.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the decay curve layer to the cumulative nuclear stability model

lessons.title: Nuclear Equations: Writing and Balancing Radioactive Decay

quiz.prompt: A uranium-238 nucleus (nucleon number 238, proton number 92) decays by emitting an alpha particle (nucleon number 4, proton number 2). Which daughter nucleus forms?
choices: Protactinium-238 (nucleon number 238, proton number 91)
Thorium-236 (nucleon number 236, proton number 90)
Thorium-234 (nucleon number 234, proton number 90)
Plutonium-242 (nucleon number 242, proton number 94)
quiz.rationale: Nucleon number and proton number are both conserved. 238 - 4 = 234 and 92 - 2 = 90, and Z = 90 is thorium.
quiz.placement: Predict: prompt card with the partially written equation ²³⁸₉₂U → ??? + ⁴₂He and the N vs Z grid

quiz.prompt: Radium-226 (nucleon number 226, proton number 88) is found in pitchblende ore with uranium. It decays by alpha emission. What is the nucleon number of the daughter nucleus?
quiz.rationale: An alpha particle carries away 4 nucleons, so the daughter has 226 - 4 = 222 nucleons. The daughter is radon-222.
quiz.placement: Evidence Activity 2 — Guided Trio Practice, Card A (α-decay of ²²⁶₈₈Ra)

quiz.prompt: Carbon-14 (nucleon number 14, proton number 6), used to date charcoal and bone, decays by beta-minus emission. Which equation is correctly balanced?
choices: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e
¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₆C + ⁰₋₁e
¹⁴₆C → ¹³₇N + ⁰₋₁e
¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₅B + ⁰₋₁e
quiz.rationale: Nucleon number stays 14. The proton number must balance: 6 = 7 + (-1). So the daughter is nitrogen-14, with proton number 7.
quiz.placement: Evidence Activity 2 — Guided Trio Practice, Card B (β-minus decay of ¹⁴₆C)

quiz.prompt: Cobalt-60 decays by beta-minus emission to an excited nickel-60 nucleus. The excited nucleus then emits a gamma ray and becomes a nickel-60 nucleus with less energy. What happens to the nucleon number and proton number of the nickel nucleus when it emits the gamma ray?
choices: The nucleon number stays the same and the proton number rises by 1
The nucleon number falls by 4 and the proton number falls by 2
The nucleon number falls by 1 and the proton number stays the same
Neither number changes; the nucleus only loses excess energy
quiz.rationale: A gamma ray is energy, not a particle with mass or charge. Nucleon number and proton number stay the same and the nucleus de-excites.
quiz.placement: Evidence Activity 2 — Guided Trio Practice, Card C (γ-emission from ⁶⁰₂₈Ni*)

quiz.prompt: Uranium-238 has 146 neutrons and 92 protons, so N/Z = 146/92 = 1.59. After alpha decay the daughter thorium-234 has N/Z = 144/90 = 1.60. What can you conclude about this single alpha step?
choices: The N/Z ratio hardly changes, so this single alpha step does not necessarily bring the nucleus closer to the belt of stability
It makes the nucleus completely stable
It moves the nucleus much closer to the belt of stability
The N/Z ratio doubles, so the nucleus moves far from the belt
quiz.rationale: The ratio changes only from 1.59 to 1.60. Alpha decay mainly reduces the size of a heavy nucleus. Thorium-234 is still unstable and decays further.
quiz.placement: Explain: plotting ²³⁴₉₀Th on the N vs Z grid and annotating the α-decay arrow

quiz.prompt: In beta-minus decay a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton, and an electron is emitted. Thorium-234 decays to protactinium-234 this way. How do the neutron number (N) and proton number (Z) of the nucleus change?
choices: N and Z both stay the same
N decreases by 1 and Z increases by 1
N increases by 1 and Z decreases by 1
N decreases by 2 and Z decreases by 2
quiz.rationale: One neutron becomes one proton, so N falls by 1 and Z rises by 1. The nucleon number stays constant. This moves a neutron-rich nucleus down and to the right, towards the belt of stability.
quiz.placement: Explain: plotting ²³⁴₉₁Pa and drawing the second arrow labelled 'β-decay' on the N vs Z grid

quiz.prompt: Pitchblende ore left in complete darkness next to photographic film exposes the film, even though the film is in a closed container. Which explanation is best?
choices: Alpha particles from uranium-238 pass easily through the container and expose the film
The uranium atoms lose heat energy, and the heat darkens the film
The rock stores sunlight and releases it slowly as light
Uranium nuclei decay into daughter nuclei, some of which emit beta and gamma radiation that pass through the container, while alpha particles are stopped
quiz.rationale: Uranium-238 decays by balanced nuclear equations into unstable daughters such as thorium-234 and protactinium-234, which emit beta and gamma radiation. These penetrate the container and expose the film; alpha particles are stopped.
quiz.placement: Explain: written 3–4 sentence explanation of what is happening inside the pitchblende ore

quiz.prompt: Uranium-238 (proton number 92) decays through a long series to stable lead-206 (proton number 82). The series has 8 alpha decays. Each alpha decay lowers the proton number by 2, and each beta-minus decay raises it by 1. How many beta-minus decays are in the series?
quiz.rationale: After 8 alpha decays the proton number is 92 - 8 × 2 = 76. To reach 82, the series needs 82 - 76 = 6 beta-minus decays.
quiz.placement: Uranium decay series chart (homework or opening of Lesson 6): counting 8 alpha and 6 beta steps from U-238 to Pb-206

lessons.title: Nuclear Fission and Fusion: Unlocking the Energy Inside the Rock

quiz.prompt: In the PhET simulation, a single neutron is fired at a uranium-235 nucleus and the nucleus undergoes fission. Which list correctly describes what is produced?
choices: Only energy, because the uranium nucleus disappears completely
Two smaller nuclei only, because the neutrons are absorbed and never released
Two smaller nuclei (fission fragments), two or three neutrons and energy
One larger nucleus and a flash of light, with no other particles
quiz.rationale: Fission splits a heavy nucleus into two smaller fragments and releases 2–3 neutrons plus energy. These neutrons are what make a chain reaction possible.
quiz.placement: Activity A, Step 1: fire a single neutron at a U-235 nucleus

quiz.prompt: A single neutron hits a uranium-235 nucleus in a block of uranium-235. Soon many nuclei are splitting. What best explains why the reaction keeps going?
choices: Each fission adds new uranium to the block, so there is always more fuel
The first neutron keeps bouncing between nuclei and splits each one in turn
The energy released changes the uranium into a different element, which then splits
The neutrons released by each fission can strike other uranium-235 nuclei and split them
quiz.rationale: Each fission releases 2–3 neutrons, and each of these can cause another fission. This cascade is called a chain reaction.
quiz.placement: Activity A, Step 2: enable 'Chain Reaction' mode and fire one neutron

quiz.prompt: Control rods are lowered into a nuclear reactor core. What do they do, and why is this important in a power plant?
choices: They absorb neutrons, which slows the chain reaction so that it stays controlled
They cool the steam so that the turbine can turn faster
They turn the uranium into a stable element so that it stops being radioactive
They add extra neutrons so that more energy is produced
quiz.rationale: Control rods absorb neutrons, so fewer fissions are triggered. This lets operators keep the chain reaction steady in a reactor, unlike in a weapon where it is left to run away.
quiz.placement: Activity A, Step 3: 'Nuclear Reactor' tab, adding control rods

quiz.prompt: Cooking ugali is a chemical reaction, and the total mass at the end is the same as at the start. In a nuclear reaction such as fission, what is different?
choices: The products have slightly more mass than the starting nucleus because energy is added to them
The products have slightly less mass than the starting nucleus, and the missing mass has become energy
The missing mass escapes as a gas that is too light to measure
The mass is the same, but the energy comes from the neutrons escaping as steam
quiz.rationale: In nuclear reactions the products weigh slightly less than the starting nucleus. The 'missing' mass (mass defect) is converted to energy by E = mc², and it is not material that escapes.
quiz.placement: Part B: Mass Defect and E = mc² (worked example)

quiz.prompt: Using E = mc² with c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, how much energy is released when 2 grams (0.002 kg) of mass is completely converted to energy?
choices: 9 × 10¹³ J
quiz.rationale: E = mc² = 0.002 × (3 × 10⁸)² = 0.002 × 9 × 10¹⁶ = 1.8 × 10¹⁴ J. The mass must be in kilograms and c must be squared.
quiz.placement: Part B: Mass Defect and E = mc² (worked example: 1 gram becomes 9 × 10¹³ J)

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly compares nuclear fission and nuclear fusion?
choices: Fission joins light nuclei such as hydrogen isotopes, and fusion splits heavy nuclei such as uranium-235
Fission splits a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235, while fusion joins light nuclei and releases more energy per kilogram of fuel
Fission releases more energy per kilogram of fuel than fusion, because it splits the nucleus
Both processes split heavy nuclei, but fusion needs no heat or pressure
quiz.rationale: Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus. Fusion is the joining of light nuclei, needs extreme heat and pressure, and releases even more energy per kilogram of fuel.
quiz.placement: Part A: Fission vs. Fusion Comparison Table

quiz.prompt:
In this fission equation, how many neutrons (x) are released?
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + x ¹₀n
choices: 4 neutrons
1 neutron
2 neutrons
3 neutrons
quiz.rationale: The mass numbers on the left add up to 235 + 1 = 236. On the right, 141 + 92 = 233, so x = 236 − 233 = 3 neutrons. The atomic numbers balance: 56 + 36 = 92.
quiz.placement: Model: add a FISSION PATHWAY with a balanced equation to the cumulative nuclear model

quiz.prompt: Kenya's Nuclear Power and Energy Agency (NuPEA, formerly KNEB) is in the news. What is its role in Kenya's energy planning?
choices: It mines uranium in Kwale County for export
It controls the water released from the Turkwel hydroelectric dam
It runs the Olkaria geothermal power stations and sells electricity to households
It leads Kenya's planning for nuclear energy, including a proposed 1,000 MW nuclear power plant
quiz.rationale: NuPEA is the agency that plans Kenya's nuclear power programme, including the proposed 1,000 MW plant. Olkaria (geothermal) and Turkwel (hydro) are separate existing energy sources.
quiz.placement: Activity B: Video Explainer (slide about NuPEA and Kenya's nuclear ambitions)

lessons.title: Applications, Safety, and Unit Review: Closing the Case of the Invisible Killer

quiz.prompt: A piece of pitchblende (uranium ore) is left on photographic film inside a light-proof, dark container. When the film is developed it is fogged. Which explanation is the most complete and correct?
choices: Uranium nuclei in the ore are unstable because their neutron-to-proton ratio is outside the belt of stability, so they decay and emit penetrating radiation that passes through the container and exposes the film.
Chemical reactions between the rock and the air inside the container produce heat that darkens the film.
The rock is stable, but it absorbs energy from the container and re-emits it as sound waves that affect the film.
The rock stored sunlight during the day and slowly released it as light in the dark.
quiz.rationale: The unstable nuclei spontaneously decay and emit radiation (alpha, beta, gamma), and the more penetrating radiation passes through the container to expose the film. No light, heat or chemical reaction is involved.
quiz.placement: Predict: final complete explanation of the pitchblende rock and film phenomenon

quiz.prompt: A factory makes aluminium sheets and uses a radioactive source on one side of the moving sheet and a detector on the other side to check the thickness continuously. Why is a beta source the best choice?
choices: Beta particles are partly absorbed by the sheet, so the count reaching the detector goes up or down as the thickness changes.
Alpha particles pass easily through metal sheets, so they give the strongest and clearest reading.
Gamma rays are completely stopped by the sheet, so the detector reading shows the thickness directly.
Beta particles are completely stopped by any sheet, so the detector reads zero when the thickness is correct.
quiz.rationale: Alpha is stopped by even thin material, so no reading would reach the detector, and gamma passes through almost unchanged, so the reading would hardly change. Beta is partly absorbed, so the detector count changes with thickness.
quiz.placement: Station 3: Industrial Thickness Gauging

quiz.prompt: The Homo habilis fossil found at Koobi Fora, Lake Turkana, is about 1.8 million years old. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5,730 years. Why can carbon-14 dating NOT be used on this fossil?
choices: Carbon-14 has such a long half-life that it has barely started to decay in the fossil.
Fossils gain new carbon-14 from the soil as they get older, so they always appear young.
The fossil is more than 300 half-lives old, so almost no carbon-14 remains to be measured.
Carbon-14 is only found in volcanic ash and not in living things.
quiz.rationale: 1,800,000 ÷ 5,730 is about 314 half-lives, so the carbon-14 left is too small to measure. A isotope with a much longer half-life, such as potassium-40 (1.25 billion years), is more suitable.
quiz.placement: Station 4: Carbon-14 Dating (Koobi Fora fossil)

quiz.prompt: At a research centre in Kenya, stored maize is treated with gamma rays from cobalt-60 to kill weevils. After the treatment, what is true about the maize?
choices: The maize is not made radioactive, because gamma rays pass through it and leave no radioactivity behind.
The maize stays radioactive for as long as the half-life of cobalt-60, so it is unsafe to eat.
Only the weevils become radioactive, while the maize itself is unaffected.
The maize is radioactive for a few days and then becomes safe.
quiz.rationale: Gamma irradiation damages the cells of pests but does not make the food radioactive. This is different from food contaminated with radioactive dust.
quiz.placement: Station 2: KALRO Crop Irradiation

quiz.prompt: A nurse works near a gamma source that gives a dose rate of 80 µSv/h at a distance of 1 m. By the inverse square law, what is the dose rate if she moves to a distance of 2 m from the source?
choices: 40 µSv/h
10 µSv/h
20 µSv/h
160 µSv/h
quiz.rationale: Doubling the distance cuts the dose rate to one quarter: 80 ÷ 2² = 80 ÷ 4 = 20 µSv/h. Halving it to 40 µSv/h is the common mistake of treating it as a simple inverse relationship.
quiz.placement: Part A: Radiation Safety Design (inverse square law mini-lesson)

quiz.prompt: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. Waste from a thyroid treatment unit is kept until its activity falls below 1% of the original. What is the shortest time, in whole half-lives, after which this is true?
choices: 8 days
80 days
48 days
56 days
quiz.rationale: After 6 half-lives the activity is 1/64 (about 1.6%), still above 1%. After 7 half-lives it is 1/128 (about 0.8%), which is below 1%. So 7 × 8 = 56 days.
quiz.placement: Part A: Radiation Safety Design (I-131 waste disposal half-life calculation)

quiz.prompt: A radiographer in a Kenyan hospital works with a gamma source. Which set of actions best follows the ALARA principle (As Low As Reasonably Achievable)?
choices: Stand close to the source but only for a short time, because gamma rays are harmless without contact.
Wear thin cotton clothing, since radiation is only dangerous if the source is touched.
Spend as little time as possible near the source, stay as far away as practical, and use shielding such as lead or thick concrete.
Use the strongest source possible and stay close so that the work is finished quickly, without shielding.
quiz.rationale: ALARA keeps exposure as low as reasonably achievable by combining less time, more distance and shielding. Gamma rays are very penetrating, so dense materials like lead or concrete are needed.
quiz.placement: Part A: Radiation Safety Design (ALARA safety plan for the nuclear medicine unit)

quiz.prompt: During the class discussion, a student asks: "Why does a piece of pitchblende keep emitting radiation day after day without ever running out?" Which answer is correct?
choices: The rock takes in energy from sunlight every day, which keeps it radioactive.
Uranium-238 has a very long half-life (about 4.5 billion years), so only a tiny fraction of its nuclei decay each day and the activity stays almost constant.
The rock only seems to emit radiation because the photographic film is slowly sending energy back.
Radioactive decay is quickly refilled by new uranium nuclei that the rock makes from the air.
quiz.rationale: Half-life explains why the rock seems to never stop. With a half-life of billions of years, very few nuclei decay in any given day, so the radiation continues for an extremely long time with no outside energy input.
quiz.placement: DQB Closure Ceremony: class consensus answer to the driving question (half-life element)
